nameStory: White-tubed Colicroot gets its name from the small white tubular flowers that cluster along its tall stem, and its historical use as a folk remedy for colic and stomach troubles. The 'root' part refers to its underground rhizomes that were harvested for medicinal purposes. It's also called unicorn root, perhaps because the single flowering spike rising from a ground-hugging rosette resembles a mythical unicorn's horn.
description: White-tubed Colicroot is a perennial wildflower that starts life looking like a small fountain of narrow, yellowish-green leaves arranged in a flat rosette at ground level. From this humble beginning, it sends up a single, impressive flowering stalk that can reach over 3 feet tall, topped with dozens of tiny white tubular flowers. The plant spreads slowly underground through rhizomes, sometimes forming small colonies in suitable habitat.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Bright yellowish-green leaves up to 8 inches long arranged in a flat rosette at ground level, narrow and strap-like with a smooth texture that feels almost waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white tubular flowers about the size of your pinky nail, densely packed along the upper portion of a single tall stem, each flower shaped like a miniature white bottle

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single flowering stalk rises dramatically from a ground-hugging leaf rosette, creating a distinctive 'exclamation point' appearance in the landscape

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small dry capsules that taper to a point at the tip, turning brown as they mature and containing tiny seeds that rattle when shaken

habitat: Look for White-tubed Colicroot in moist, acidic areas with sandy or peaty soils, especially in pine barrens, bog edges, and wet meadows. It thrives in areas that stay consistently moist but not waterlogged, often in partial sun where the soil has a spongy, organic feel underfoot.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright yellowish-green in rosettes, easily spotted against darker soil. The flowering stalk begins to develop in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time when the tall white flower spikes are most visible and distinctive. The tiny white flowers open from bottom to top along the stem.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and develop into pointed seed capsules. Leaves may begin to yellow but often remain somewhat green into winter.
seasonality.winter: Leaves die back, leaving only the dried flower stalks standing like brown exclamation points above the snow, with seed capsules still attached.

funFact: Despite being called 'colicroot,' this plant is actually more closely related to lilies than to any medicinal herbs, and its underground rhizomes are so bitter that early settlers nicknamed them 'blazing star' because they literally made your mouth burn when chewed.
confusionNotes: The ground-hugging leaf rosette might be confused with young iris plants, but iris leaves are blue-green and arranged like a fan, while colicroot leaves are yellowish-green and spread flat like a star. Remember: 'Yellow star on the ground, colicroot has been found.'
contextualKnowledge: This plant has many folk names including 'true unicorn' and 'stargrass,' which can be confusing since there are other unrelated plants called stargrass. The 'true unicorn' name distinguishes it from 'false unicorn' (a completely different plant), showing how common names can create botanical mix-ups.
compareHints: White-tubed Colicroot is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique in the region. Within its plant family, it's distinguished from other bog plants by its distinctive ground rosette of yellowish-green leaves and single tall flowering spike with tiny white tubular flowers, rather than the larger, more colorful blooms of related species.
